newsitem.title: FRANCE: Generale des Eaux back in profit, aims for record.
newsitem.headline: Generale des Eaux back in profit, aims for record.

text.p: Generale des Eaux, France's biggest water, construction and communications group, said on Thursday it had returned to profit in 1996 and saw profits hitting a record level in 1997.
Chairman Jean-Marie Messier said the group would make a 1997 net profit of at least five billion francs ($888 million), which would be a record in the company's history.
Generale des Eaux reported a 1996 net attributable profit of 1.95 billion francs against a 1995 loss -- mainly due to property and restructuring write-downs -- of 3.69 billion francs in 1995.
It raised its dividend by 6.7 percent to 12 francs per share. Sales were up 3.4 percent at 165.9 billion francs.
"In 1996, we were a little bit better and a little bit quicker than we forecast," Messier said. In October it had forecast a 1996 net profit of 1.8 billion francs.
"In 1997, we will have a group which is geared for action, with lower debts, restructured and reorganised," he added.
Messier said he expected operating income to rise by more than 10 percent in 1997, from 3.8 billion francs in 1995.

Debts would be cut by a further 13 billion to 32 billion francs which, together with a rise in shareholders funds of at least 10 billion to 43 billion francs, would cut the debt ratio to 75 percent from 150.

Messier said that, following a deal in which it obtained 30 percent in Havas and the creation of telecoms group Cegetel, Generale des Eaux would in the year 2000 draw 50 percent of its sales and profits from its traditional environment activities -- water and waste management as well as rail transport.

Construction would make up 25 percent of sales and 15 percent of results. It now accounts for 40 percent of sales. Communication -- television and telecoms -- will account for 25 percent of sales and 35 percent of profit.
Messier said that the final agreement on establishing the Cegetel unit would be signed at the end of April.
British Telecom will have a 26 percent stake in Cegetel, which aims to become the main rival to France Telecom after market liberalisation in 1998.

Generale itself will have a nine percent direct stake in the unit. It also has a 70 percent stake in the Transtel joint venture, with SBC Communications Inc of the U.S. holding the remaining 30 percent.
Transtel will have a 50 percent stake in Cegetel.

Messier said that he had three main priorities with Havas in 1997 -- the sale of Havas Voyages, the sale of Havas's ODA unit to France Telecom and a normalisation of relations between Havas and Belgium's Albert Frere.
Havas and its pay-television unit Canal Plus fell out with Frere, who has a big stake in Luxembourg's CLT, after a series of changing European television partnerships in 1995 and 1996.
CLT is now part of the TPS French digital satellite television venture which rivals CanalSatellite in France.
Messier said that, while a deal to combine the two would have been possible a year ago, it now made "absolutely no sense". ($1=5.630 French Franc)
